facts.nickname: The Silver State (also the Battle Born State)
facts.name_origin: Spanish for 'snowy' or 'snow-covered,' for the snow on the mountains in winter (as in the Sierra Nevada).

government.chambers: Nevada Senate (21 senators, 4-year terms) and Nevada Assembly (42 members, 2-year terms); the Legislature has had these numbers since 1983. After the 2018 election, Nevada became the first state with a female majority in its legislature.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term), who holds the 'supreme executive power' of the state.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Nevada (a chief justice and six associate justices).
government.local: 16 counties plus Carson City, an independent city that is not part of any county.
government.constitution: Constitution of 1864, still in use. In 1864 territorial Governor James Nye had the whole constitution telegraphed to Washington, D.C.; it is the longest telegram in the National Archives. It promised that 'there shall be in this state neither slavery nor involuntary servitude.'
government.kid_line: "Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by this State or any of its political subdivisions on account of race, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, disability, ancestry or national origin." (Nevada Constitution, Article 1, Section 24, added in 2022)

long_ago.about: The Washoe may have entered the Great Basin from California as many as 4,000 years ago. They camped by Lake Tahoe and Washoe Lake, along the Truckee, Carson, and Walker rivers, and near springs in the Pine Nut Hills, and have made fine baskets for thousands of years.

Northern Paiute bands of about a hundred people moved with the seasons, living in huts of willow poles covered with brush and reeds. They gathered pine nuts from piñon trees in fall, fished, and hunted rabbits in winter.

Numic-speaking peoples, including the Southern Paiute, began moving into the Great Basin around the year 1000. Their homeland covered more than thirty million acres, including southern Nevada, and small groups of three to five households moved with the plant harvests and animal migrations.

With the Paiute and Washoe, the Shoshone lived on the land that is now Nevada before Europeans came. Western Shoshone communities today include the Te-Moak Tribe's Battle Mountain, Elko, South Fork, and Wells bands.

More than 1,000 years ago, Puebloan people farmed in the Moapa Valley of southern Nevada. At Pueblo Grande de Nevada (the 'Lost City') they built adobe houses, some with more than 100 rooms, and mined salt to cook with and trade. The Hopi claim these people as ancestors.

today.about: Reservation of 475,000 acres about 35 miles northeast of Reno, surrounding Pyramid Lake.

first_peoples.today_note: A State of Nevada (Department of Native American Affairs) list names 28 tribes, bands, colonies, and community councils, mostly Paiute, Shoshone, and Washoe; the Te-Moak Tribe and the Washoe Tribe each include several bands or communities. Some, like the Washoe Tribe, the Fort McDermitt Paiute-Shoshone Tribe, and the Confederated Tribes of the Goshute Reservation, have lands in Nevada and a neighboring state.
sites: Lost City Museum in Overton, which tells the story of Pueblo Grande de Nevada; much of the site was covered by Lake Mead after Hoover Dam was built, so archaeologists rushed to record it.
Pyramid Lake, a 27-mile-long desert lake inside the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation.

history.event: Ancestors of the Washoe may have come into the Great Basin from California, settling around Lake Tahoe and the rivers flowing east from the Sierra Nevada.
Basketmaker and then Puebloan people live in the Moapa Valley, building pit houses and later large adobe pueblos at the 'Lost City.'
Numic-speaking peoples, ancestors of the Paiute and Shoshone, spread across the Great Basin.

Spanish colonists bring a slave trade into the Great Basin. Raiders capture Southern Paiute people, especially children, to sell, and the trade grows after the Old Spanish Trail opens between New Mexico and the Pacific coast.
Raphael Rivera, a scout on Antonio Armijo's trading route from New Mexico, is the first to name Las Vegas, in a report to New Mexico's governor.
After the Mexican-American War, the United States takes the region from Mexico, which had governed it since Mexico won independence from Spain in 1821.

Mormon settlers build Mormon Station (now Genoa), the first permanent non-Native settlement, as a trading post for travelers on the California Trail. Chinese miners also arrive in western Nevada in the 1850s.

Silver is discovered at the Comstock Lode, bringing a flood of miners. The invasion destroys the Paiute way of hunting and gathering, and Paiute and Washoe people face starvation in the winter of 1859 to 1860.
Violence by newcomers against the Paiute leads to the Pyramid Lake War. The Paiute leader Numaga argues for peace before and after the fighting.
Congress creates Nevada Territory from the western part of Utah Territory.
During the Civil War, Nevada's constitution, which bans slavery, is telegraphed to President Lincoln. Nevada becomes the 36th state on October 31, earning the name 'Battle Born.'
After the Bannock War, the U.S. forces many Paiute people who had stayed peaceful off the Malheur Reservation and moves them hundreds of miles north to the Yakama Reservation in Washington.

trailblazers.name: Sarah Winnemucca (Thocmetony, 'Shell Flower')
trailblazers.group: Northern Paiute woman, writer and activist
trailblazers.text: Sarah Winnemucca worked as an interpreter between Paiute people and the U.S. Army and spoke out about the injustice her people faced. Her 1883 book, Life Among the Piutes, was the first book published by an American Indian woman. Later she started a school where Paiute children learned in their own language and in English.

trailblazers.name: Dat So La Lee (Dabuda, Louisa Keyser)
trailblazers.text: Born in Carson Valley, Dabuda became famous for her degikup baskets, which start with a small round base, swell out wide, and narrow again at the top. She used her designs like words to tell a story, and she signed bills of sale with her handprint. She wove for about thirty years until her death.

trailblazers.name: Anne Martin
trailblazers.text: Born in Empire City, Anne Martin founded the history department at the University of Nevada. As president of the Nevada Equal Franchise Society, she led the campaign that won Nevada women the right to vote on November 3, 1914. She ran for the U.S. Senate in 1918 and 1920.

trailblazers.name: Lubertha Johnson
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, nurse and civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: Southern Nevada's first Black nurse, Lubertha Johnson led the Las Vegas NAACP and signed the Consent Decree to end job discrimination in the hotel and casino industry. She founded Operation Independence, which included Clark County's first Head Start program. Her motto: 'Education is the key to independence.'

trailblazers.name: Woodrow Wilson
trailblazers.text: In 1966 Woodrow Wilson became the first African American elected to the Nevada Legislature. He led the Las Vegas NAACP and helped pass Nevada's Fair Housing Law, which outlawed discrimination in selling homes. He also co-founded a credit union to lend money to Black families and other minorities. Later, in 1984, he resigned from the Clark County Commission after pleading guilty to taking a bribe.

trailblazers.name: Velma Johnston ('Wild Horse Annie')
trailblazers.text: Born in Reno, Velma Johnston saw wild horses being hauled to slaughter in 1950 and started a campaign to protect them. She won state and federal laws protecting wild horses and burros in the West.

landforms: Basin and Range: many north-south mountain ranges with valleys between them
Great Basin, covering most of the state
Sierra Nevada (Carson Range) on the western edge
Boundary Peak, the highest point (13,147 feet)
Wheeler Peak (13,063 feet) in Great Basin National Park
waters: Pyramid Lake and Walker Lake, desert lakes with no outlet to the sea
Humboldt River, which ends in the Humboldt Sink
Truckee, Carson, and Walker rivers flowing east from the Sierra
Colorado River and Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the country
geography.regions: Nevada lies almost entirely in the Basin and Range region: most of it is the Great Basin, whose rivers never reach the ocean, with the Mojave Desert in the south and the Sierra Nevada on the western edge.

ecosystems.name: High mountain forests (Great Basin National Park)
ecosystems.about: Great Basin bristlecone pines grow in harsh, windy groves just below the tree line. They are the oldest non-clonal species on the planet and can live thousands of years; their dense wood resists insects and rot.

ecosystems.name: Mojave Desert
ecosystems.about: Desert tortoises live in burrows among creosote bushes and can survive more than a year without drinking water. Their numbers have dropped as much as 90 percent in some areas, and they are a threatened species.

ecosystems.name: Sagebrush valleys and piñon hills
ecosystems.about: Basin floors are covered with sagebrush (the state flower), bunchgrass, and scrub, while piñon and juniper woodlands grow on the hills. Piñon pine nuts, gathered each fall, were an essential food for the Paiute, who also hunted rabbits in the valleys.

science.weather: Nevada is the driest state, with only about 7 inches of rain a year on average, because it sits in the rain shadow of the Sierra Nevada. Summers can be extremely hot (record 125°F at Laughlin in 1994) and winters very cold in the north (record -50°F at San Jacinto in 1937). Nevada is the fourth most earthquake-active state, and wildfires burn about 400,000 acres a year.
science.resources: Tourism is Nevada's largest employer, and mining is a major industry: Nevada is one of the world's largest gold producers and is called the Silver State for its silver history.
science.highlight: Ichthyosaurs: 225 million years ago a warm ocean covered central Nevada. Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park holds the most abundant and largest known remains of these giant marine reptiles, Nevada's state fossil.

g3_ss.title: Nevada's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Carson City, Las Vegas, Reno, and tribal lands on a map; learn what the Legislature, Governor, and Supreme Court do and that Nevada's tribes govern themselves.

g3_ss.title: Nevada's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Washoe baskets, Paiute seasonal camps and pine nut harvests, and Shoshone communities; students design a basket pattern that tells a story.

g3_ss.title: Nevada Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Story cards for Sarah Winnemucca, Dat So La Lee, Anne Martin, Lubertha Johnson, Woodrow Wilson, and Wild Horse Annie.

g45_ss.title: Nevada's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Compare Washoe, Northern and Southern Paiute, Shoshone, and Ancestral Puebloan ways of life in a desert land, using the Lost City and Pyramid Lake.

g45_ss.title: Spain, Mexico, and the Trails
g45_ss.plan: The Old Spanish Trail and the slave trade that targeted Paiute children, Rafael Rivera naming Las Vegas, Mexican rule, and the 1848 transfer to the United States.

g45_ss.title: Silver, War, and Statehood, 1851–1878
g45_ss.plan: Mormon Station, Chinese miners, the Comstock Lode and its harm to Native peoples, the Pyramid Lake War, and the 'Battle Born' statehood telegram that banned slavery.

g3_sci.title: Desert Survivors
g3_sci.plan: How desert tortoises, sagebrush, and bighorn sheep survive heat and little water; build a burrow model.

g3_sci.title: The Oldest Trees
g3_sci.plan: Bristlecone pines and tree rings: count rings on a slice and learn why slow growth helps them live thousands of years.

g3_sci.title: Sea Monsters in the Desert
g3_sci.plan: Ichthyosaurs and the ancient ocean that covered Nevada; how ocean fossils ended up on dry land.

g45_sci.title: Rain Shadows and the Driest State
g45_sci.plan: Model how the Sierra Nevada wrings water from Pacific air, leaving Nevada dry; compare rainfall maps.

g45_sci.title: Basin and Range and Earthquakes
g45_sci.plan: How the crust stretching apart forms ranges and valleys and causes earthquakes; earthquake safety.

g45_sci.title: Where Rivers End
g45_sci.plan: Terminal lakes like Pyramid Lake and the Humboldt Sink: where the water goes, evaporation, and why salts build up.
